summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for modeling and storing alarms, giving network management systems a standard way to keep track of fault conditions reported by devices.

eli5.summary: It is a standard notebook where a device writes down alarms, so managers can read them the same way on any device.

what is the itu alarm mib
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a device describe its possible alarms and keep a list of the ones currently active.

tldr.problem: Managers that only poll objects or wait for notifications cannot cheaply watch many devices, cannot tell what went wrong while they were not looking, and struggle to relate polled objects, notifications and problems.
tldr.mechanism: The ALARM-MIB defines alarm models (which notifications mean which alarm state), a table of active alarms, statistics, and a table of recently cleared alarms. An optional ITU-ALARM-MIB adds ITU-style details.
tldr.outcome: A manager can ask a device which alarms are active at any time, including problems that began while it was out of contact.

today: RFC 3877 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text gives no deployment information.

sections.title: Why SNMP Needs Alarm Management
sections.content:
In traditional SNMP management, problems are found by polling MIB variables, by waiting for a Notification, or by both. The RFC lists the weaknesses. Managers watching large numbers of entities cannot afford to poll many objects on each device. Managers that need high reliability cannot tell whether problems occurred while they were not monitoring. And it takes time to work out how polled objects, received Notifications and real problems relate, sometimes leaving an incomplete picture.

The memo describes a method of alarm management in SNMP and supplies the MIB objects to support it. It builds on the Internet-Standard Management Framework, with a MIB module written in SMIv2.
sections.eli5: Asking every device over and over 'any problems?' is tiring, and you miss things while you are away. A board that lists problems solves both.

sections.title: Alarm Terms and Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC defines its vocabulary carefully. An alarm is a persistent indication of a fault, and a fault is a lasting error or warning condition. An alarm state is a stage in the life of an alarm; at a minimum the states are raise and clear, and they may carry ITU perceived severity values such as cleared, indeterminate, critical, major, minor and warning. An active alarm has been raised but not cleared, and the alarm detection point is the entity that detected it.

The architecture is modular. A generic Alarm MIB can be used alone or with extra alarm modelling information, such as the ITU Alarm MIB, and the active alarm tables can be extended with more detail per alarm instance. The cost of supporting alarm management is meant to be proportional to the features an implementation supports. Alarms SHOULD be modelled so Notifications are sent on alarm clear.
sections.eli5: An alarm is a problem that stays. It starts as 'raised' and ends as 'cleared', and in between it sits on the board.

sections.title: The Generic ALARM-MIB
sections.content:
The ALARM-MIB consists of alarm models and lists of active and cleared alarms:

  • alarmModelTable holds what applies to every instance of an alarm: the possible states and the OID of the Notification tied to each state. If a Notification is not in this table, it is not an alarm state transition. Its rows are read-create, so managers can adjust the models.
  • alarmActiveTable lists the alarms occurring now. It is meant to be queried when a device is discovered or rediscovered.
  • alarmActiveVariableTable keeps the Notification variable bindings for those alarms.
  • alarmActiveStatsTable holds current and total raised alarm counts and the time of the last raise and clear, per named alarm list.
  • alarmClearTable holds recently cleared alarms, up to alarmClearMaximum of them. When the limit is reached, the entries with the earliest clear time are removed.

The MIB also defines two generic Notifications, alarmActiveState and alarmClearState, for cases where no existing Notification fits.
sections.eli5: The device keeps a rulebook of problems it knows about, a board of problems happening now, and a short list of ones that were just fixed.

sections.title: How Alarms Relate to Notifications and Resources
sections.content:
Alarm states can be modelled three ways: with traditional Notifications (matched by Notification OID and optionally an offset and value pair in a varbind), with the generic alarmActiveState and alarmClearState Notifications, or with no Notifications at all. Not every Notification is an alarm; purely informational ones, such as a note that a configuration operation was done, are not represented. Setting alarmModelNotificationId to { 0 0 } means nothing is logged or sent for that state transition.

To say where a problem is, alarmActiveResourceId is built from the Notification varbinds using alarmModelVarbindSubtree and alarmModelResourcePrefix. For a linkDown alarm, setting the subtree to ifIndex makes the interface the resource, so two alarms on the same interface can be recognised as the same resource.

For varbinds, sysUptime and snmpTrapOID are always stored as entries 1 and 2 of the active alarm variable table, whichever PDU type carried the Notification, so index values are adjusted by two. In the linkDown case, the third varbind is always ifIndex.
sections.eli5: Each alarm note says what is wrong and which part is broken, like 'the third door is jammed', so two notes about the same door can be matched up.

sections.title: The ITU Alarm Extension
sections.content:
A second module, the ITU-ALARM-MIB, adds alarm information from the models in ITU M.3100, X.733 and X.736. It follows the modular design: for each row in the ITU model table there is one row in alarmModelTable, and pointer objects such as alarmModelSpecificPointer and alarmActiveSpecificPointer link the generic rows to the specific ones.

Its tables are ituAlarmTable (possible alarms), ituAlarmActiveTable (currently occurring ones) and ituAlarmActiveStatsTable (statistics). The IANA section makes IANA responsible for the enumerations in the IANAITUEventType and IANAItuProbableCause textual conventions. Probable cause value 0 is reserved and MUST NOT be assigned, and values 1 to 1023 are reserved for causes that correspond to ITU-T probable cause.
sections.eli5: This is an optional extra page for the telephone-industry way of describing a problem, with extra labels such as how serious it is.

sections.title: Relation to Other MIBs and Distribution
sections.content:
The Alarm MIB is meant to complement the Notification Log MIB (RFC 3014) but can be used independently. The active alarm table is defined in a manner similar to nlmLogTable, and alarmActiveLogPointer can point to the matching log index. The log can serve as a hedge against lost alarms and support historical alarm management. There is no direct relation or dependency with the Event MIB.

Which managers receive Notifications is controlled through the SNMP-TARGET-MIB and SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB in RFC 3413. For distributed management, the MIB can run both on the device and on a mid-level manager, which can keep a separate named alarm list per managed device.
sections.eli5: The alarm board works nicely next to the diary the device already keeps, and a middle manager can keep a separate board for each device it looks after.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, including alarmModelNotificationId, alarmModelRowStatus and alarmClearMaximum, may be sensitive without protection. Setting alarmClearMaximum too low may cause security related alarm history to be lost early. Adding or removing alarm models needs careful planning, and removing a model should delete that model's related alarms.

The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Access can be controlled per named alarm list using view-based access control. For locally generated Notifications the system MUST use the security credentials tied to each alarm model, while for remotely generated ones it SHOULD NOT apply access control. It also warns that alarmActiveContextName can reveal SNMPv1 community strings.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change the rulebook could hide problems, so only trusted people should get the pen, and messages should be locked.
